summary: Deep dive into split-eviction behavior observed in Crestline's private deployment under long-context workloads. Discussion covered prefix affinity, warmup strategies, paging to disk, batching interplay, and whether Dedicated pools or Private on-prem config reduces tail latency and cost. Action items to run benchmarks and exchange configs.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give it a little bit until folks join in but, uh, the purpose today is to... dig into the split-eviction pattern you guys saw and try to reproduce it and, um, figure out mitigations.
[00:12] Jordan Miles: Yep thanks Alex. We had a spike last week where the tail latency doubled for some of our long context sessions, and we saw a lot more KV evictions than we'd expect.
[00:25] Priya Nair: Okay quick qual first — you're on the private deployment in our VPC, right? Not hosted?
[00:31] Marina Soto: Correct, private control plane with VPC peering, we run on-prem GPUs behind, uh, the Redwood private agent.
[00:39] Devon King: And we do 7k average context for a portion of inference calls, with a mix of short prompts and a long history prefix per customer.
[00:48] Priya Nair: Got it. That mixed workload + long prefixes is classic for prefix reuse issues. Quick question — are you using persistent KV backing or ephemeral in-memory only?
[00:58] Jordan Miles: It's in-memory primarily with spill to our NFS-backed storage in extreme cases. We saw page-to-disk activity at a higher rate.
[01:07] Samir Patel: When you say page-to-disk, is it the Redwood runtime spilling KV to the tokenstore or your infra level paging?
[01:14] Marina Soto: Looks like the runtime initiated KV spillback to NFS, the logs show 'kv-pager-start' from the agent.
[01:21] Priya Nair: Okay interesting. Two quick hypotheses: one, a warmup gap where reused prefixes are evicted between bursts; two, eviction hysteresis caused by uneven batching patterns leading to local hotness across GPUs.
[01:34] Anita Rao: Can you explain hysteresis in plain terms?
[01:37] Priya Nair: Sure — hysteresis here means when a prefix becomes hot, it stays hot for some time; but if evictions are too aggressive on a per-shard basis, you can oscillate: prefix gets evicted, then a later request misses, causes a heavy fetch and repopulation, then it gets evicted again. That thrash increases latency and IO.
[01:55] Jordan Miles: That's exactly the pattern. We saw a loop where the same prefix was loaded repeatedly and that correlates with the longer tail latency.
[02:04] Alex Chen: Would you be able to share a small histogram of token lengths per request? That helps us pick prefetch thresholds and batch windows.
[02:11] Marina Soto: We'll send that after the call.
[02:15] Priya Nair: Cool. Another note — prefix affinity across GPU shards matters. If the routing distributes prefixes randomly, you lose locality. Are you using session affinity or round-robin?
[02:26] Devon King: Currently we use round-robin to balance GPU load, because some of our models have uneven compute.
[02:32] Priya Nair: That explains a lot. Round-robin can spread a hot prefix across shards and cause each shard to think the occupancy is low and evict more aggressively. Affinity routing keeps a prefix on the same shard so the local KV stays warm.
[02:45] Jordan Miles: But we were worried affinity would create hot-spotting and imbalance.
[02:49] Samir Patel: Right, it's a tradeoff. We recommend a hybrid: soft-affinity with fallback. Pin a prefix for a TTL, but allow rebalancing if shard is overloaded. That reduces thrash while keeping balance.
[03:02] Priya Nair: Exactly — also prefetch heuristics: on first miss, fetch adjacent prefixes or history chunks that are commonly accessed together. That amortizes the cold-fetch cost. But prefetch increases memory use so it's a knob to tune.
[03:14] Anita Rao: Prefetch seems risky for cost. How do you measure ROI?
[03:18] Priya Nair: We instrument token fetch latencies and count the hit-rate delta after prefetch. Typical measure: delta in average token fetch time vs incremental memory used. We target hit-rate improvements above a set ROI threshold — e.g., 15% hit-rate lift per 10% memory growth.
[03:32] Marina Soto: Also, we saw eviction patterns tied to our autoscaler spikes during batch windows. We batch-heavy at 2am for nightly processing.
[03:39] Alex Chen: Batching can align many requests and cause synchronized eviction pressure if the batch window causes simultaneous writes. Staggering batch windows or using continuous batching with jitter helps.
[03:49] Jordan Miles: We do use continuous batching on the runtime but the job triggers a heavy burst which correlates to evictions.
[03:56] Priya Nair: For heavy background batches, you can route them to dedicated capacity or throttle KV priority. Redwood supports priority routing so foreground low-latency requests preserve cache residency.
[04:07] Devon King: Are there settings we can toggle in our config quickly to test?
[04:10] Priya Nair: Yes — two low-friction changes: increase per-prefix TTL and enable soft-affinity with TTL of X minutes, and enable prefetch for the top-N prefixes per customer. We can also reduce eviction aggressiveness by raising the eviction watermark by 10%.
[04:22] Jordan Miles: Sounds good. Would that require downtime?
[04:25] Priya Nair: No config change is live; you can roll it with canary to a small subset.
[04:29] Alex Chen: We'll share a canary plan. Also, we want to run a reproducible benchmark with your prompt set so we can see end-to-end tail latency and IO.
[04:37] Marina Soto: On security side — we need to ensure KMS keys remain customer-managed. Will the benchmark require exposing keys?
[04:44] Samir Patel: No, benchmark can run against synthetic keys or using a read-only telemetry bucket; we won't require key sharing. We will, however, ask for sample traffic and token length histograms.
[04:54] Jordan Miles: About paging — is there a recommended backing store? NFS seems to be a bottleneck for us.
[04:59] Priya Nair: NFS is okay for occasional spill, but for high spill rate you'd want a low-latency persistent store — local NVMe or an S3-like object store with fast read latency. Ideally, prefer a distributed KV-backed disk with concurrent read capability. For on-prem, local NVMe per shard is best.
[05:14] Devon King: We can provision NVMe on a subset of nodes.
[05:17] Anita Rao: What's the quantization impact here? We're using 4-bit quant on our weights to save memory.
[05:22] Priya Nair: Quantization affects speed and memory footprint mostly for the model tensors; KV storage still stores activations/kv in float16 or quantized representation depending on runtime. If KV is kept quantized, you reduce memory but increase decode overhead. Our runtime supports quantized KV variants but there is a small CPU decode cost which can slightly raise token latency on misses.
[05:41] Jordan Miles: So more quant reduces memory pressure but could add a decode hit during repopulation?
[05:45] Priya Nair: Correct — it's again an ROI. If spills are causing repeated loads, quantizing KV may reduce spill frequency enough to offset decode cost. We can measure during benchmark.
[05:55] Alex Chen: Quick note — earlier you mentioned some logs indicating 'kv-evict-split' entries. Can you share a few? That helps Priya triage the exact code paths.
[06:04] Marina Soto: We'll upload the logs to the shared folder, link in the follow-up email.
[06:09] Samir Patel: From Redwood side, we'll instrument two further metrics: per-prefix eviction rate, repopulation latency, and shard-local miss-ratio over time. That should show hotspots.
[06:20] Jordan Miles: Perfect.
[06:22] Priya Nair: Also, consider smaller training of the affinity hash — we can change the hash function so prefixes that share a customer or conversation bucket map together, improving locality without full pinning.
[06:34] Devon King: That's neat — any pitfalls?
[06:36] Priya Nair: If the mapping is too coarse you'll get hot shards again. It's about tuning bucket size.
[06:42] Alex Chen: Ok let's talk timeline. We'll run a benchmark in your staging with your sample traffic, we'll trial soft-affinity and raised eviction watermark, and then compare metrics.
[06:51] Jordan Miles: How long do you need?
[06:53] Priya Nair: We can get an initial run in 48–72 hours from receipt of histograms and logs.
[06:58] Alex Chen: Action items recapped — Priya attach prefetch guide, Alex schedule bench, Marina upload logs and token histograms, Devon capture traces. Any other items?
[07:08] Anita Rao: Security review? We'll need SOC2 controls doc and KMS integration patterns.
[07:12] Samir Patel: We'll attach the SOC2 summary and the KMS integration notes to the follow-up.
[07:17] Jordan Miles: One more question — for cost, if we move noisy-nightly batches to Dedicated, how do we estimate incremental cost?
[07:24] Alex Chen: We'll provide a cost simulation: e.g., dedicated pool pricing vs hosted request cost, factoring in lower repopulation IO and lower tail latency. We'll put the model in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[07:34] Marina Soto: Great. Also link any console dashboards so we can see ttl/eviction metrics.
[07:39] Priya Nair: We'll share a template dashboard and a set of alerting rules for eviction spikes.
[07:44] Alex Chen: Ok final quick recap then we'll wrap.
[07:47] Alex Chen: Recap: run benchmark, try soft-affinity + higher eviction watermark + controlled prefetch, compare tail latency and IO, share security docs. Follow-ups in email.
[07:58] Jordan Miles: Thanks all. This was super helpful.
[08:01] Anita Rao: Thanks.
[08:03] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the run window.
[08:07] [call ended]
